def add_runs(p, text, bold=False, italic=False, size=None):
    # simple markup: **bold** and *italic*
    import re
    parts = re.split(r'(\*\*[^*]+\*\*|\*[^*]+\*)', text)
    for part in parts:
        if not part:
            continue
        if part.startswith('**') and part.endswith('**'):
            r = p.add_run(part[2:-2]); r.bold = True; r.italic = italic
        elif part.startswith('*') and part.endswith('*') and len(part) > 2:
            r = p.add_run(part[1:-1]); r.italic = True; r.bold = bold
        else:
            r = p.add_run(part); r.bold = bold; r.italic = italic

issue('B-1', 'The Brief Inverts Rev. Proc. 93-27, Which Provides That Receipt of a Profits Interest Is Generally *Not* a Taxable Event',

 ['Rev. Proc. 93-27 § 4.01 provides that, if a person receives a profits interest for services to or for the benefit of a partnership in a partner capacity, the IRS **will not treat the receipt as a taxable event**. Section 4.02 lists three exceptions: (1) the profits interest relates to a substantially certain and predictable stream of income from partnership assets, *such as income from high-quality debt securities or a high-quality net lease*; (2) the partner disposes of the interest within two years; or (3) the interest is a limited partnership interest in a publicly traded partnership. Rev. Proc. 2001-43 supplements it. The “determinable value” language is not in the revenue procedure; it echoes the pre-1993 *Diamond*/*Campbell* case law that Rev. Proc. 93-27 was issued to address. The Ridgeline Opinion describes Rev. Proc. 93-27 correctly (§ III.D).',

  'When Treasury proposed the § 707(a)(2)(A) regulations in 2015, the preamble announced that the IRS *intended* to issue a revenue procedure adding a new exception to Rev. Proc. 93-27 for profits interests issued in conjunction with a partner forgoing payment of a substantially fixed amount (i.e., fee waivers). 80 Fed. Reg. 43652 (July 23, 2015) [cite-check]. To my knowledge, no such revenue procedure has issued. The government\'s position therefore requires an exception the IRS itself acknowledged does not yet exist.',

That is irreconcilable with the FPAA\'s adjustments.'],

Exposing that the government and its expert have described an authority as standing for the opposite of what it says will color the Court\'s view of every other legal proposition in the motion, and it eliminates an entire theory (Ashford Opinion 3).',

issue('B-2', 'The Brief Misstates the Treas. Reg. § 1.707-2(c) Factors, Omits Factor (4), Imports the § 704(b) “Transitory Allocation” Framework, and Ignores That the Regulation Is Only Proposed',
 ['Arg. IV.A.2: “The Treasury Regulations provide a six-factor test . . . . The government submits that each applicable factor weighs decisively in favor of recharacterization.” The Brief then labels Factors (1), (2), (3), (5) and (6) and, in place of Factor (4), inserts a heading “The Priority Allocations Constitute Transitory Allocations Lacking Substantial Economic Effect,” relying on Treas. Reg. § 1.704-1(b)(2)(iii). Arg. IV.A.5: “Every applicable factor . . . weighs in favor” — listing five.'],
 ['**Status.** Section 1.707-2 is a *proposed* regulation (REG-115452-14, 80 Fed. Reg. 43652 (July 23, 2015)) that has never been finalized. By its terms it would apply to arrangements entered into or modified after final regulations are published [cite-check proposed effective date provision]. Proposed regulations are not binding and receive no deference, although they may be considered for their persuasive value. The Brief repeatedly calls them “the Treasury Regulations” and “the implementing regulations.”',
  '**Content.** Prop. Treas. Reg. § 1.707-2(c) makes **significant entrepreneurial risk** the most important factor ((c)(1)) and then lists five secondary factors: whether the service provider (2) holds a transitory or short-duration interest; (3) receives allocations and distributions in a time frame comparable to a non-partner service provider; (4) became a partner primarily to obtain tax benefits not otherwise available; (5) has a continuing interest in general partnership profits that is small relative to the allocation; and (6) receives different allocations for different services with significantly different entrepreneurial risk [cite-check exact text]. The government\'s Factors (2) (“guaranteed payment or preferred return”), (3) (“converting ordinary income to capital gain”), (5) (“relatively fixed in relation to the services”), and (6) (“subject to a ceiling”) do not appear in the proposed regulation. Several are drawn loosely from the (c)(1) list of facts that create a presumption of insufficient risk, and one is inverted: under the proposed regulation it is a *cap* (“capped allocations . . . if the cap would reasonably be expected to apply in most years”) that signals insufficient risk, so the *absence* of a ceiling cannot support recharacterization.',
  '**Omitted factors favor HCP.** The factors the Brief skips are the ones HCP wins: HCP\'s interest in the Funds (through its wholly owned GPs) is long-term, not transitory; the GPs were partners with carried interests independent of the waiver, so HCP did not “become a partner” to obtain tax benefits; and the value of HCP\'s continuing interest in general Fund profits (including its 20% carry, Ridgeline § III.A.2 Factor 6) is not small relative to the priority allocations.',
  '**Imported framework.** The § 704(b) transitory-allocation rule (Treas. Reg. § 1.704-1(b)(2)(iii)(c)) asks whether an *allocation among partners* is likely to be offset by *subsequent allocations* so that capital accounts end where they would have been. A waived management fee is not a partnership allocation, so it cannot be an “offsetting allocation.” Moreover, the remedy for an allocation lacking substantial economic effect is reallocation in accordance with the partners\' interests in the partnership, not recharacterization of capital gain as ordinary income — and the FPAA made no § 704(b) adjustment (Quillen Decl. ¶ 61). The Ridgeline Opinion specifically warned that the two frameworks are “distinct” and “should not be conflated” (§ III.A.4).'],
 'Critical',
 'The § 707(a)(2)(A) argument is the government\'s lead theory. A Court that sees the government has mis-described the test it asks the Court to apply, omitted the factors that favor the taxpayer, and substituted an unrelated framework is unlikely to find the issue suitable for summary judgment.',
 ['Set out the proposed regulation\'s actual text in a table and walk through each factor, with record citations. Note the regulation\'s proposed status in one sentence, but argue primarily that HCP prevails even under the IRS\'s own proposed standard (see caution below).',
  '**Caution:** the Ridgeline Opinion also cites “Treasury Regulations § 1.707-2(c)” as if final and uses its own, non-textual factor labels (e.g., “clawback,” “reasonably certain”). The opposition should rely on the regulatory text, not on Ridgeline\'s labels, and should not overemphasize the “proposed” point in a way that suggests HCP\'s adviser misunderstood the law. The (c)(1) presumption list also contains facts the government may invoke in reply (see Issue D-3).']
)

issue('B-5', 'The § 707(c) Guaranteed-Payment Remedy Is Legally Unavailable and Is Not the Basis of the FPAA',
 ['Part V.A: “The priority allocations are, in substance, guaranteed payments within the meaning of IRC § 707(c). They were determined without regard to the partnership\'s income . . . . Recharacterization of the priority allocations as guaranteed payments is therefore the appropriate remedy.” Ashford Decl. ¶¶ 37–48 (Opinion 2).'],
 ['Section 707(c) reaches only payments “determined without regard to the income of the partnership.” The priority allocation is payable “solely from the Fund\'s net long-term capital gains” (Election Forms § 3), and if there are none the allocation is zero for that year and may never be paid. The government concedes as much (SUMF ¶ 10: “payable solely from realized long-term capital gains”), and Professor Ashford acknowledges that the allocations “appear to be ‘determined with regard to the income of the partnership’” (¶ 42). An amount computed by reference to partnership income is a distributive share, not a guaranteed payment [cite-check: Treas. Reg. § 1.707-1(c); Rev. Rul. 69-180].',
  'Sections 707(a) and 707(c) are mutually exclusive: § 707(a)(2)(A) treats the recipient as a non-partner; § 707(c) treats the recipient as a partner receiving a fixed payment. The Brief asks for both.',
  'The FPAA rests on § 707(a)(2)(A) and economic substance (Quillen Decl. ¶ 61). A § 707(c) recharacterization is a new theory on which the government should bear the burden (Issue B-15).',
  'A guaranteed-payment remedy would carry correlative consequences the government ignores (a § 162 deduction or § 263 capitalization at the Fund level, which reduces the LPs\' gains). The government seeks only the one-sided adjustment to HCP.'],
 'Significant',
 'The remedy section is where the government tells the Court what judgment to enter. A remedy that is unavailable as a matter of statutory text, and inconsistent with the liability theory, is a strong reason to deny the motion as framed.',
 ['Argue that, because the government itself cannot identify which provision governs the recharacterization, it has not shown entitlement to judgment as a matter of law. Use the statutory text and Ashford ¶ 42\'s concession.']
)

issue('B-6', 'The Economic Substance Argument Does Not Satisfy § 7701(o) or Address Second Circuit Law',
 ['Arg. IV.C (relying on *Gregory*, *ASA Investerings* (D.C. Cir.), *Frank Lyon*; TOA also lists *Coltec* (Fed. Cir.) and *Klamath* (5th Cir.)). Ashford Decl. ¶ 27 (“I focus primarily on whether HCP had a substantial non-tax business purpose”).'],
 ['**No relevance analysis.** Section 7701(o)(5)(C) provides that whether the doctrine is “relevant” to a transaction is determined as if § 7701(o) had never been enacted. The Brief simply assumes relevance. The legislative history (Joint Committee on Taxation, JCX-18-10, at 152–53 (2010) [cite-check]) states that codification was not intended to disturb basic business choices respected under longstanding practice. The choice between taking compensation as a fee or as a profits-based partnership allocation is precisely such a choice; Congress has repeatedly legislated in this space (§§ 707(a)(2)(A), 1061) without treating profit-share compensation as lacking substance. LB&I\'s own directive requires examiners to analyze relevance and obtain executive-level approval before asserting the codified doctrine [cite-check: LB&I-4-0711-015 (July 15, 2011), as updated]; the record is silent on compliance.',
  '**Objective prong never analyzed.** Section 7701(o)(1)(A) asks whether the transaction changes the taxpayer\'s economic position in a meaningful way. The Brief\'s analysis is almost entirely about purpose (“The Fee Waiver Arrangement Lacks a Genuine Business Purpose”), followed by a conclusory sentence that nothing changed (Arg. IV.C.3). The record shows that HCP exchanged a fixed fee payable regardless of performance for an unsecured, non-interest-bearing claim subordinated to the realization of net long-term capital gains and extinguished on liquidation — and, for Fund V, actually received nothing (Issue A-3).',
  '**Purpose prong misstated.** The statute requires “a substantial purpose” apart from tax effects, not the absence of a tax purpose. The Brief repeatedly argues that tax savings were the “sole” purpose, but its citations do not support that, and the Ridgeline Opinion documents three non-tax purposes (Issue A-14). Purpose and intent are classic jury-type questions ill-suited to summary judgment.',
  '**Wrong circuit.** The Brief cites no Second Circuit economic substance authority. The opposition should address *Gilman v. Commissioner*, 933 F.2d 143 (2d Cir. 1991), and *Bank of New York Mellon Corp. v. Commissioner*, 801 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2015) [cite-check]. (Note: *BNY Mellon* is pro-government on its facts and emphasizes pre-tax profit potential; we should distinguish it rather than ignore it.) *Frank Lyon* in fact supports respecting the form of a transaction “imbued with tax-independent considerations” and involving genuine third-party economic stakes.'],
 'Critical',
 'Economic substance is the government\'s broadest theory and the predicate for its § 7701(o)-based penalty argument. The missing relevance and objective-prong analyses are legal deficiencies, and the purpose prong presents a fact dispute.',
 ['Structure the response in three steps: (1) the doctrine is not relevant to a choice of compensation form within a statutory regime Congress has specifically addressed; (2) even if relevant, the objective prong is satisfied as a matter of record fact (Fund V; liquidation cut-off; subordination); (3) the purpose prong presents, at minimum, a genuine dispute (Ridgeline § III.C.3; declarations of Hargrove, Sato, LP witness).',
  'Request, through discovery or a Rule 56(d) declaration if needed, any LB&I relevance analysis and approval for asserting the doctrine.']
)

issue('B-13', 'The Substantial Authority and Negligence Arguments Apply the Wrong Standards and Anachronistic Authority',

issue('B-14', 'The Government Ignores BBA Procedure and the Timeliness and Validity of the FPAA',
 ['Prelim. Stmt.; SUMF ¶¶ 7, 30–31 (FPAA served on Sato as “Tax Matters Partner”; TY 2018 return filed September 15, 2019, “pursuant to an extension”). Quillen Decl. ¶¶ 11, 55–63. The Brief contains no discussion of §§ 6231 or 6235.'],
 ['**Regime.** TY 2018–2020 are BBA years. The notices required are a notice of proposed partnership adjustment (NOPPA) and a notice of final partnership adjustment (FPA), mailed to the partnership and its partnership representative (§ 6231(a)). The record identifies the PR as Elliot R. Hargrove (Ex. 7), yet the FPAA was “served upon Ms. Sato in her capacity as Tax Matters Partner” (Quillen Decl. ¶ 59).',
  '**Missing NOPPA / premature FPA.** Under § 6231(b)(2)(A), an FPA may not be mailed earlier than 270 days after the NOPPA unless the partnership waives. The record describes only a “30-day letter” dated February 7, 2022, a protest on March 9, 2022, and an FPAA on June 15, 2022 — 128 days later (Quillen Decl. ¶¶ 60–61). If the February 7 letter was the NOPPA, the FPA was premature (270 days would have run on November 4, 2022); if it was not, the record shows no NOPPA at all.',
  '**Limitations.** Under § 6235(a), the period for making partnership adjustments is generally three years from the later of the return filing date or due date (with extensions keyed to the NOPPA in § 6235(a)(2)–(3)). For TY 2018 (filed September 15, 2019) the three-year period ran on **September 15, 2022**; the FPAA was within that period *if valid*. But if the FPAA is invalid for procedural defects, a new FPA for TY 2018 would now be time-barred, and TY 2019 (filed on extension, presumably September 15, 2020) likely expired September 15, 2023, absent a § 6235(b) extension or NOPPA-based extension. TY 2020 may remain open until approximately September 15, 2024. The TY 2019 and TY 2020 filing dates are not in the record.',
  '**Election out.** HCP appears to have six partners, all individuals (Quillen Decl. ¶ 10). Such a partnership may elect out of the BBA under § 6221(b) on a timely filed return. The PR designation on the TY 2018 return suggests no election out for that year, but we must confirm for each year. If HCP elected out for any year, a partnership-level FPA would be a nullity for that year.',
  '**Candor point.** HCP\'s timely petition (September 8, 2022, within 90 days of June 15, 2022, § 6234(a)) shows actual receipt, and courts are generally reluctant to invalidate a notice that the taxpayer actually received and timely contested. The strength of the argument depends on whether a NOPPA issued, whether HCP waived the 270-day period, and whether any extension was signed.'],
 'Critical',
 'Contingent on verification. If the procedural defects are established, they could eliminate the TY 2018 and TY 2019 adjustments ($31,250,000, or 65.6% of the total) regardless of the merits. Even if not ultimately dispositive, the government\'s failure to address timeliness is a gap in its summary-judgment showing if HCP has pleaded the defense.',
 ['**Immediately** pull the administrative file: all IRS letters (including any Letter 5893 NOPPA), any 270-day waiver, any extension of the § 6235 period, the FPA itself and its mailing addresses, Forms 1065 for all three years (PR designation; Schedule B-2 election out), and the Form 2848.',
  'Confirm that our answer/petition pleaded limitations and notice defects as affirmative defenses (Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(c)). If not, evaluate a prompt Rule 15(a) motion.',
  'Confirm that the § 6234(b) jurisdictional deposit for district court review was made and in what amount (see Part X).',
  'If the facts support it, consider a cross-motion for partial summary judgment on TY 2018/2019 timeliness; otherwise raise it as a genuine dispute precluding judgment.']
)
